methods.description: Read the axes/scales and project between the requested time or distance and the appropriate point/segment, retaining units and the stated journey branch.

Interpret rising,flat and falling segments of distance from a fixed start; identify away,stop,return and compare moving steepness on the same scales, then match the sequence to a journey story. A straight moving segment has steady speed.
Read start/end times of each horizontal stop and subtract, adding durations when more than one stop is requested; keep clock time and elapsed duration distinct.
For a journey along the same route, read every positive distance covered from the changes in distance from the start and add them; a return adds travelled distance rather than subtracting it.
For simultaneous journeys along the same route with the same distance reference, use the crossing as same place/time and read both coordinates from the axes.
Identify a graph segment moving to an earlier time; one journey cannot run backwards in time or have two different distances at the same time. Explain this in ordinary journey language.

theory.intro: A **distance–time graph** shows a journey, with time on the horizontal axis. Read the vertical-axis label and scales: it may show **distance from the start** or **total distance travelled**.
facts: On the **same axes**, the steeper moving segment shows faster travel, whether it rises or falls. A straight moving segment shows steady speed.
To read a distance, go up from the time axis to the line, then across; to read a time, go across then down.
On a graph of **distance from the start**, the highest point gives the greatest distance from the start.
The length of a horizontal segment is how long the stop lasted.
Along the same route, add the distance covered in each moving stage to find the **total distance travelled**.
Time moves forwards along a journey graph. A segment going back to an earlier time cannot show a real journey.
When two journeys use the same route and distance reference, the crossing of their lines shows where and when they meet.
Returning lowers the **distance from the start**, but the **total distance travelled** keeps increasing.
steps: Read the axes and their scales.
Find the segment or point the question is about.
State the reading, or describe what that part of the journey shows.

workedExamples.solution_text:
(a) Go up from $3.5$ hours to the line, then across to the distance axis. Asha is $17$ km from the start.
(b) Go across from $15$ km to the rising line, then down to the time axis. She reaches $15$ km after $3.25$ hours.
(c) She stops from $1.5$ to $2.5$ hours and from $4$ to $5$ hours.
Total stopped time $=(2.5-1.5)+(5-4)=2$ hours.
(d) From $5$ to $6.5$ hours the distance from the start falls to $0$, so she returns to the start. This segment is steeper than the first, so she travels faster on the return.
(e) She travels $9$ km out, then $21-9=12$ km farther out, then $21$ km back.
Total distance $=9+12+21=42\text{ km}$.
Her distance from the start falls on the return, but the total distance she has travelled does not fall.

Graph **A**.
Its line first rises steeply: travelling quickly away from home.
The horizontal segment shows the wait.
The gentler falling segment shows a slower return and ends at $0$, back at home.
Graph B shows the slower outward stage first and the faster return afterwards.

They pass where the two lines cross: both riders are at the same distance from the start at the same time.
Read down from the crossing to the time axis: $3$ hours.
Read across to the distance axis: $18$ km.
They pass after $3$ hours, $18$ km from Maya’s starting point.

After $2$ hours, the line goes back to $1.5$ hours, an earlier time.
Time cannot go backwards during the journey.
The graph also shows two different distances from the start at the same time.
It cannot show one traveller’s real journey.

foundation.solution_text: The graph is horizontal from $1$ hour to $2$ hours, so the distance from home is not changing: the car was stopped between $1$ hour and $2$ hours.

The horizontal segment runs from $0.5$ hours to $1$ hour.
The stop lasts $1-0.5=0.5$ hours.
$0.5\times60=30$ minutes.
Stage A rises most steeply, and the steeper the line the faster the journey, so the van was travelling fastest during stage A.
The graph slopes down from $2$ hours to $4$ hours, so the distance from the start is falling: Leo was walking back between $2$ hours and $4$ hours.

development.solution_text: The journey needs a line sloping up (walking away), then a horizontal line (waiting), then a line sloping back down to zero (arriving home). Only graph A has all three, so the answer is graph A.

The taxi drives $30$ km out, then $30-10=20$ km back, then $40-10=30$ km out again.
Total distance $=30+20+30=80\text{ km}$.
The line after the stop is steeper than the line before it, and the steeper the line the faster the journey, so Sam was travelling faster after the stop.

Ben stops from $1$ hour to $1.5$ hours and from $2.5$ hours to $3.5$ hours.
The stops last $1.5-1=0.5$ hours and $3.5-2.5=1$ hour.
Total stopped time $=0.5+1=1.5$ hours.

mastery.solution_text:
For the first $60$ minutes the line rises steeply, so Dana walks away from home and reaches $4$ km.
From $60$ to $75$ minutes the line is horizontal, so she stops.
From $75$ to $120$ minutes the line rises less steeply, so she keeps walking away from home but more slowly, reaching $6$ km.
From $120$ to $150$ minutes the line is horizontal again, so she stops a second time, and because the line never slopes down she never heads back home.

After the first stage the line moves to the left, back to an earlier time.
That would mean the cyclist is at two different distances at the same time, and that time runs backwards, so no real journey can look like this.

The hikers pass where the two lines cross, because there they are the same distance along the track at the same time.
Reading down from the crossing point gives $2$ hours, and reading across gives $8$ km.

options.why: Chose the first sloping segment, where the car was driving away from home.
Chose the last sloping segment, where the car was driving again.
Read the parked time as running from its start to the end of the whole trip.

questions.solution_text: The graph is horizontal from $1.5$ hours to $2.5$ hours, so the distance from home is not changing and the car is parked over that interval.

options.why: Read the horizontal part of the graph instead of going up to the line at $3$ hours.
Read the distance at the end of the journey rather than at $3$ hours.
Read the line half an hour too far along, at $3.5$ hours.

questions.solution_text: Going up from $3$ hours to the line and across to the distance axis lands on $60$, so the train had travelled $60$ km.

options.why: Read the time Marco set off again rather than the time he reached $9$ km.
Read the time at the end of the run instead of at the $9$ km line.
Read the time at the first bend, where only $6$ km had been covered.

questions.solution_text: Going across from $9$ km to the line and down to the time axis lands on $45$, so Marco was $9$ km from the warehouse after $45$ minutes.

options.why: Read the time at which the wait ended instead of how long the wait lasted.
Gave the time for the whole trip rather than the length of the horizontal segment.

questions.solution_text: The journey needs a steep line up, then straight away a gentler line back down to zero. Graph B is the only one with the steeper leg first and no horizontal segment.

options.why: Read the final distance from the depot instead of adding every stage of the trip.
Added the first $24$ km and the $18$ km driven back, but left out the final $12$ km.
Gave the distance of the first stage only.

questions.solution_text:
The bus drives $24$ km out, then $24-6=18$ km back, then $18-6=12$ km out again.
Total distance $=24+18+12=54\text{ km}$.

options.text: After $1$ hour, $10$ km from Port A
After $1$ hour, $20$ km from Port A
options.why: Read the crossing height as the distance still to go, measuring back from Port B.

options.text: After $2$ hours, $20$ km from Port A
options.why: Followed only the Port A ferry's line to $2$ hours instead of finding where the two lines cross.

options.text: After $1.5$ hours, $15$ km from Port A
options.why: Took the midpoint of the route and of the time rather than reading the crossing point.

questions.solution_text:
The ferries pass where the two lines cross, because there they are at the same place at the same time.
Reading down from the crossing point gives $1$ hour, and reading across gives $10$ km.

options.why: Uses the time at which the stop ends rather than when it begins.
Reads the distance value of 1 km as though it were the time.
Uses the duration of the stop instead of its starting time.

questions.solution_text: On a distance-time graph, Molly stops when the line is horizontal. The horizontal section begins at 10 minutes, so she stopped after 10 minutes.
